name: Version control
summary: Record every change to the code as a commit, so anyone can see who changed what, when and why, and get any earlier version back.
howItWorks: A version control system keeps a repository: the full history of a project as a chain of commits. Each commit is a snapshot of the files plus who made it, when, a message saying why, and a pointer to the commit before it. A branch is a named line of commits, so people can work on separate changes at once; a merge joins two branches back together, and the tool combines the edits automatically unless two people changed the same lines (a conflict a person must resolve). Older, centralized systems such as CVS, Subversion and Perforce keep the history on one server and clients check files out from it. Distributed systems such as Git and Mercurial give every clone the whole history, so commits, branches and logs work offline, and every clone is a backup. Teams still agree on one shared copy, usually on a host like GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, where changes arrive as pull requests (GitLab calls them merge requests) that others review and that automated checks test before they are merged. Some organizations keep all their code in one repository (a monorepo), which makes changes that span many projects atomic but needs special tooling at scale; others give each service its own repository (polyrepo), which is simpler per project, but a change that spans several repositories needs several coordinated pull requests.
analogy: A lab notebook where every entry is dated and signed and pages are never torn out, and anyone can photocopy the whole book to work on at home and send their new pages back.
useWhen: Always, for source code, infrastructure definitions, configuration and documentation
Several people change the same codebase and need to review and merge each other’s work
You need to know which change broke something, and roll it back
avoidWhen: Storing large binaries, datasets or build outputs directly in Git; use Git LFS, an artifact registry or object storage
Committing secrets: anything pushed stays in the history even after a later commit deletes it
example: A five-person team keeps a web app in one Git repository on GitHub. A developer creates the branch `fix-login-timeout`, makes two commits on a train with no network, and pushes when back online. She opens a pull request; CI runs 400 tests in four minutes and a teammate approves it. A week later a bug report points at login, and `git log` and `git blame` show exactly which commit touched that line and why.

source: git switch -c fix-login-timeout        # a new branch from main
# edit files, then record the change
git commit -m "Extend login session timeout to 30 minutes"
git push -u origin fix-login-timeout   # share it, then open a pull request
git blame src/session.ts               # which commit last changed each line

sections.title: Centralized or distributed
sections.intro: Both models track commits and branches; they differ in where the history lives and what that makes cheap.

rows.label: Where history lives
values: On one server; clients hold a working copy
In every clone; one copy is the agreed shared one

rows.label: Offline work
values: Commits, logs and diffs against history need the server
Commit, branch, log and diff locally

rows.label: Branches
values: A copy of a directory, made on the server
A pointer to a commit, created nearly instantly

rows.label: Access control
values: Per path: Subversion can grant read or write on a single directory
Per repository: anyone who can read gets the whole history

rows.label: Binary files
values: Subversion’s locking stops two people editing an unmergeable image at once
Needs an add-on such as Git LFS for large files

rows.label: Failure mode
values: The server is a single point of failure
Every clone is a full backup

story: Version control started at Bell Labs. In 1972 Marc Rochkind began the Source Code Control System (SCCS), which stored each file’s changes as deltas so any earlier version could be rebuilt. In the early 1980s Walter Tichy at Purdue wrote RCS, which also stored revisions as deltas and, like SCCS, expected people to lock a file before editing it. In 1986 Dick Grune posted the shell scripts that became CVS, which let several people edit their own copies of a set of directories at once and merged their changes afterwards; two years later Brian Berliner rewrote it in C, and it spread widely.

By 2000 CVS’s limits were obvious to CollabNet, which hired developers to write a replacement that kept the basic ideas of CVS “but without the bugs and misfeatures”. Subversion hosted its own code from August 2001. It stayed centralized: one server held the history. Meanwhile the Linux kernel, which had passed patches around by email for a decade, adopted the proprietary distributed tool BitKeeper in 2002. In April 2005 the arrangement broke down and its free licence was withdrawn, and Linus Torvalds wrote that he would have to find an alternative.

He made the first commit of Git on April 7, 2005, and the kernel moved to it nine days later; Matt Mackall announced Mercurial the same month with similar goals. Git handed every developer the full history and made branches nearly free. Hosts such as GitHub, which opened in April 2008, built review around the pull request: a page for discussing a branch before it is merged. By 2022, 94% of respondents to Stack Overflow’s developer survey used Git.

choices.choice: Copy, modify, merge instead of lock, modify, unlock
choices.why: SCCS and RCS made people lock a file before changing it, which serialized work. CVS let everyone edit their own copy and merged the results, betting that real conflicts are rare. Almost every system since has made the same bet, and kept locking only for binary files.

choices.choice: Every clone holds the full history
choices.why: With BitKeeper, Torvalds wrote, the people around him had a much easier time merging with his tree and sending him theirs. Git and Mercurial kept that model: everyone has a full repository, works offline, and no single server’s loss means losing history.

In Subversion a branch is a copy of a directory made on the server. In Git a branch is a small file holding the hash of a commit, so creating or switching one is nearly instant, and a short-lived branch for every change became normal.

Google’s internal Mondrian tool, and later Rietveld, Gerrit and GitHub’s pull requests, made a second pair of eyes a step in the workflow rather than an afterthought. Hosts can now require approvals and passing checks before a branch may be merged.
